justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias for what appears to be a broad equity index instrument (likely SPY or a similar S&P 500 tracker given the price level around $417). For the one-day horizon, I anchored close to the prevailing price with a slight upward drift, reflecting the general tendency of equity markets to carry a small positive daily expected return and assuming no major overnight catalysts were already priced in. For the one-week estimate, I projected a marginally higher level, consistent with a roughly flat-to-slightly-positive drift over five trading sessions. The one-month estimate extends that drift further, reflecting the long-run equity risk premium compounded over approximately 21 trading days while staying conservative about the magnitude of movement.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to historical volatility patterns at each time horizon. For a single day, realized volatility on major equity indices tends to run around 1–1.5% on calm days, which supported a relatively tight band of roughly plus or minus 2% around the point estimate. Over one week, uncertainty compounds and I widened the interval to reflect that a week can easily contain a meaningful macro surprise, earnings catalyst, or geopolitical development. The one-month interval is substantially wider because monthly moves of 10–15% or more are not historically rare during periods of macro stress, and a full month encompasses multiple potential inflection points including Fed meetings, employment data, and earnings reports.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a surprise Federal Reserve policy shift — either an unexpected rate hike or a pivot signal — which has historically caused single-day moves well beyond 2% in either direction. A significant geopolitical escalation, a financial contagion event such as a banking stress episode, or a sharper-than-expected deterioration in economic data could all produce downside outcomes below my lower bounds. On the upside, a decisive resolution of a major macro overhang or a stronger-than-expected earnings season could push prices above my upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon.

Finally, it is worth acknowledging that my intervals were constructed under an assumption of roughly normal market conditions. Tail events by their nature are underrepresented in any confidence interval framework, and markets can exhibit fat-tailed behavior — meaning the true probability of extreme outcomes is somewhat higher than my intervals implicitly suggest. If realized volatility were to spike materially from the level prevailing at the time of the forecast, all three intervals could prove too narrow simultaneously, which is the classic limitation of volatility-anchored probabilistic forecasting.
